title: 02. Networking, Protocols & APIs: Long Polling

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Long polling is an HTTP request-response pattern in which the client issues a request and the server deliberately holds the response open (without sending a body) until new data is available or a timeout expires, at which point the server responds and the client immediately re-issues the request, producing near-real-time push over plain HTTP.
Long polling was the dominant technique for fake server-push before WebSockets and SSE were standardized. The mechanics are simple to describe but subtle to implement well. The client sends a normal HTTP GET to something like `/messages?since=12345`. The server receives the request, checks whether there are any new messages with id > 12345; if yes, it responds immediately with them; if no, it parks the request (typically by suspending an async handler or stashing it in a queue) and waits. When a new message arrives — 100 ms later or 25 seconds later — the server resumes the parked request, writes the new message(s) as the response body, and closes the response. The client receives the response, processes it, and immediately issues another GET to `/messages?since=<newest id>` to wait for the next message. If no message arrives within a timeout (typically 30-45 seconds), the server responds with an empty 200 OK so the client knows the connection is still alive and re-requests. The result is near-real-time push with sub-second median latency, using nothing but standard HTTP that every proxy, firewall, and browser already understands. Long polling is essentially the trick of "making the server appear to push by deliberately delaying its response to a GET."

Long polling matters because for years it was the only cross-browser, cross-network technique that worked. **Gmail Chat** (launched 2005) famously used long polling to deliver instant messages in the browser before WebSockets existed; users saw messages appear within a second of being sent, despite the underlying transport being plain HTTP/1.1 over a single connection. **Facebook Chat** (launched 2008) used long polling for years before migrating to MQTT over WebSockets as the user base exploded past hundreds of millions of concurrent users. **Twitter** used long polling for its live tweet stream and live notifications on the web well into the 2010s. The reason all of these used long polling is that WebSockets were not standardized until RFC 6455 in 2011, were not supported in all browsers until 2013, and were broken by many corporate proxies until well into the 2010s; long polling, being plain HTTP, just worked everywhere. Even today, long polling remains the universal fallback when WebSockets are blocked — Slack, Discord, and WhatsApp all ship a long-polling fallback for users behind restrictive corporate firewalls.

The trade-offs and pitfalls are significant, which is why long polling has been largely replaced by SSE and WebSockets for new systems. First, **connection overhead per cycle** — every long-poll cycle terminates with a fresh HTTP response and the next cycle begins with a fresh HTTP request, repeating all headers (cookies, auth tokens, 200-800 bytes of overhead per cycle). At one cycle per second per user, a million users generate 1M requests/second of overhead just to maintain the long-poll loop. Second, **thread or coroutine cost on the server** — a naive thread-per-request server (older Tomcat, Apache with prefork MPM, Flask's dev server) consumes one OS thread per parked request; 10k parked long polls = 10k OS threads = ~10 GB of stack memory, even if the threads are idle. Async frameworks (Node.js, Python asyncio, Go goroutines, Java Netty, Erlang processes) reduce this to a few KB per parked request, which is why the long-polling era drove the widespread adoption of async servers. Third, **head-of-line latency** — the client can only have one long poll in flight at a time (browsers historically limited 6 connections per origin), so if a poll takes 5 seconds to return a batch of messages, the client cannot start the next poll for those 5 seconds, during which new messages wait at the server. Pipelining or HTTP/2 multiplexing mitigates this but adds complexity. Fourth, **timeout handling** — the server must pick a timeout (typically 30s) that balances proxy idle-connection limits (many proxies kill idle connections at 60s) against the cost of cycling the poll; if the server picks 30s and a message arrives at 30.1s, the client gets an empty response, re-requests, and the message is delivered — but with 30s of avoidable latency if the request that returned empty was actually due to the message arriving just after the timeout.

A real-world example worth studying is Facebook Chat's architecture circa 2008-2010. The chat servers held long-poll requests open for up to 30 seconds in a custom Erlang-based subsystem that managed millions of parked connections efficiently (Erlang's lightweight processes made this feasible). When a user sent a message, the chat backend looked up the recipients, found the servers holding their long-poll connections, and signaled those servers to respond with the new message. The design scaled but had notable pain points: every cycle incurred a full HTTP request/response with cookies and auth revalidation, the connection-per-user limit forced them to multiplex many users' polls over a shared set of HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connections, and the latency tail (p99) was worse than WebSocket because of the polling cycle. Facebook eventually migrated to MQTT over WebSockets for mobile (lower bandwidth, persistent connection, native publish/subscribe semantics) and to WebSockets for web. Twitter's migration followed a similar arc — long polling → SSE for the live tweet stream → eventually a mix of HTTP/2 streaming and WebSockets. Long polling connects to many other system design concepts: it is the historical fallback for HTTP push (Phase 2 Topics 13 WebSockets and 15 SSE), it forces async server architecture (Phase 6 concurrency), it is the substrate of early chat systems like WhatsApp's predecessor architecture, and its tail-latency and back-pressure issues are an instance of the broader flow-control topic in Phase 7 reliability.

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client (browser)
    participant S as Long-Poll Server
    participant Q as Message Queue
    Note over C,S: Cycle 1 (no data ready)
    C->>S: GET /poll?since=100 (t=0)
    S->>Q: subscribe(since=100)
    Note over S,Q: request parked (async, no thread held)
    Q-->>S: no messages yet...
    S-->>C: 200 OK [] (timeout at t=30s)
    Note over C: client immediately re-requests
    C->>S: GET /poll?since=100 (t=30s)
    Note over S,Q: request parked again
    Q-->>S: msg 101 arrives (t=32s)
    S-->>C: 200 OK [{id:101, text:"hi"}]
    Note over C: client immediately re-requests
    C->>S: GET /poll?since=101 (t=32s)
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
   +-----------+   GET /poll?since=100      +-----------+
   |  Client   | -------------------------> |  Server   |
   | (browser) |                             | (async)   |
   +-----------+                             +-----+-----+
        ^                                          |
        | (no data, request held open)             | park req in
        |                                          | waiting queue
        |                                          v
        |                                  +-------+-------+
        |                                  | message queue |
        |                                  +-------+-------+
        |                                          ^
        |                                  another client
        |                                  publishes msg
        |                                          |
        |  server wakes parked request             |
        |<-----------------------------------------+
        |  200 OK [{id:101}]                       |
        |                                          |
        |  client immediately re-request:          |
        |  GET /poll?since=101                     |
        +----------------------------------------->|

   Per-cycle overhead: 1 HTTP req + 1 HTTP resp (headers repeated)
   Cycle length: 0s (instant reply if data ready) to 30s (timeout)
   Steady state: 1 outstanding request per user, forever
```

### Walkthrough
1. The client opens an HTTP GET to `/poll?since=<last_id>` with normal headers (cookies, auth, Accept: application/json). The server receives the request, parses the `since` cursor, and queries its message store for any messages newer than `since`. If messages exist, the server immediately writes a 200 OK with the JSON array of new messages and closes the response — total latency is one server round trip. If no messages exist, the server does NOT respond; instead it creates a Future/Promise (Python `asyncio.Future`, Node.js Promise, Go channel) tied to the user's `since` cursor, registers it in an in-memory map keyed by user_id, and parks the request. In an async framework, this consumes a few KB of memory and no OS thread; in a thread-per-request framework, it would consume one OS thread (~1 MB stack) per parked request, which is why long polling forced the industry to async servers.
2. When another client publishes a message (via a POST to `/publish` or an internal service call), the server's publish handler looks up the recipients, finds the parked Future for each recipient, resolves it with the new message payload, and the parked request handler wakes up, writes the 200 OK with the message, and closes the response. If the message is for multiple recipients (a group chat), the server fans out: resolve each recipient's Future, each gets a 200 OK. If a recipient has no parked request (offline or between polls), the message is persisted in their inbox queue and will be returned the next time they poll.
3. The client receives the 200 OK, processes the message(s), and immediately issues another GET `/poll?since=<newest_id>`. The cycle repeats. If no message arrives within the server's timeout (typically 30s), the server writes a 200 OK with an empty array `[]` to keep the cycle alive without making the client think the connection died. The client re-requests. If the connection actually dies (proxy timeout, network change), the client detects the closed response and re-requests with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, capped at 30s) to avoid hammering a recovering server. To avoid losing messages between cycles, the server returns messages in id order and the client always uses the highest id received as the next `since` cursor; messages published between a cycle ending and the next cycle starting are returned in the next cycle.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
**What this code covers**

- Append a message to recipient's inbox and wake any parked poll.
- Return messages newer than since.
- A long-poll client that loops: poll -> process -> re-poll.
- Long-polling chat server in pure stdlib asyncio.
- Demonstrates: parked requests, fan-out on publish,
- 30s timeout, since-cursor, backoff on reconnect.
- Per-user inbox: list of {id, from, text, ts}
- Per-user list of parked Futures waiting for messages

**Defines:** `LongPollChat`, `simulate_clients()`

```python
# Long-polling chat server in pure stdlib asyncio.
# Demonstrates: parked requests, fan-out on publish,
# 30s timeout, since-cursor, backoff on reconnect.

import asyncio
import json
import time
from collections import defaultdict

POLL_TIMEOUT = 30.0  # seconds to hold a poll open if no data

class LongPollChat:
    def __init__(self):
        # Per-user inbox: list of {id, from, text, ts}
        self.inboxes = defaultdict(list)
        # Per-user list of parked Futures waiting for messages
        self.waiters = defaultdict(list)
        # Monotonic message id counter
        self.next_id = 1
        self.lock = asyncio.Lock()

    async def publish(self, recipient: str, sender: str, text: str) -> int:
        """Append a message to recipient's inbox and wake any parked poll."""
        async with self.lock:
            msg = {"id": self.next_id, "from": sender,
                   "text": text, "ts": time.time()}
            self.next_id += 1
            self.inboxes[recipient].append(msg)
            # Wake every parked poller for this recipient.
            woken = 0
            while self.waiters[recipient]:
                fut = self.waiters[recipient].pop(0)
                if not fut.done():
                    fut.set_result(True)
                    woken += 1
            print(f"  [publish] user={recipient!r} msg_id={msg['id']} "
                  f"woke={woken} parked={len(self.waiters[recipient])}")
            return msg["id"]

    async def poll(self, user: str, since: int) -> list:
        """Return messages newer than `since`. Hold up to 30s if none."""
        async with self.lock:
            # First check: any messages already queued?
            new_msgs = [m for m in self.inboxes[user] if m["id"] > since]
            if new_msgs:
                print(f"  [poll] user={user!r} immediate hit: "
                      f"{len(new_msgs)} msgs")
                return new_msgs
            # No messages yet: park the request.
            fut = asyncio.get_event_loop().create_future()
            self.waiters[user].append(fut)
            parked = len(self.waiters[user])
            print(f"  [poll] user={user!r} parking (since={since}, "
                  f"parked={parked})")
        # Wait for either a publish (resolves fut) or a timeout.
        try:
            await asyncio.wait_for(fut, timeout=POLL_TIMEOUT)
            reason = "woken by publish"
        except asyncio.TimeoutError:
            reason = "timeout (30s)"
        async with self.lock:
            new_msgs = [m for m in self.inboxes[user] if m["id"] > since]
            # Clean up: remove this fut if still parked (e.g. timed out).
            if not fut.done():
                fut.cancel()
                if fut in self.waiters[user]:
                    self.waiters[user].remove(fut)
            print(f"  [poll] user={user!r} returning "
                  f"{len(new_msgs)} msgs ({reason})")
            return new_msgs

# --- Demo -----------------------------------------------------

async def simulate_clients():
    chat = LongPollChat()

    async def poller(user: str, since: int = 0, label: str = ""):
        """A long-poll client that loops: poll -> process -> re-poll."""
        last = since
        for cycle in range(1, 4):  # 3 cycles per client for the demo
            print(f"[{label}] cycle {cycle} GET /poll?since={last}")
            msgs = await chat.poll(user, last)
            for m in msgs:
                print(f"[{label}]   <-- msg id={m['id']} "
                      f"from={m['from']!r} text={m['text']!r}")
                last = m["id"]
            if not msgs:
                print(f"[{label}]   <-- (no messages, re-poll)")
            await asyncio.sleep(0.05)  # tiny think time before re-poll

    async def publisher():
        # Wait a moment, then publish a message to alice.
        await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
        await chat.publish("alice", "bob", "hey alice!")
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
        await chat.publish("alice", "carol", "lunch at noon?")
        # A message for bob that arrives after his first poll parks.
        await asyncio.sleep(0.1)
        await chat.publish("bob", "alice", "yo bob here")

    # alice starts polling immediately; bob also polls in parallel.
    await asyncio.gather(
        poller("alice", since=0, label="alice"),
        poller("bob", since=0, label="bob  "),
        publisher(),
    )

    # Show the final inbox state.
    print("\n--- final inboxes ---")
    for u in ("alice", "bob"):
        for m in chat.inboxes[u]:
            print(f"  {u}: id={m['id']} from={m['from']!r} "
                  f"text={m['text']!r}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("=== Long-polling chat demo (asyncio) ===\n")
    asyncio.run(simulate_clients())
```

quiz.question: What is long polling, and how does it differ from short polling?
options: Long polling: client GETs /poll?since=N; server holds the response open; when data is ready, server writes the body (typically JSON) and closes the response; client immediately re-GETs.
Choose long polling when: (1) You must support legacy proxies that buffer SSE streams or strip WebSocket Upgrade headers — long polling uses normal HTTP responses that…
The classic bug: client polls and gets msg id=100; client re-requests ?since=100; meanwhile msg id=101 is published in the gap between the response and the next request…
Short polling: the client sends GET /messages every N seconds (say 5s); the server responds immediately with whatever is queued (possibly empty); the client waits 5s and asks again.
quiz.explanation: Short polling: the client sends GET /messages every N seconds (say 5s); the server responds immediately with whatever is queued (possibly empty); the client waits 5s and asks again. Median latency to receive a new message is N/2 (2.5s on average for a 5s poll), and the client burns one HTTP request every N seconds even when nothing is happening — at 1M users × 1 req/5s = 200k requests/second of pure overhead.

quiz.explanation: A thread-per-request server (Apache prefork MPM, older Tomcat, Flask dev server, Django runserver) assigns one OS thread to each in-flight HTTP request. If the request takes 30s to respond (because it's parked waiting for a message), that thread is blocked for 30s doing nothing. OS threads are expensive: ~1-8 MB of stack each, ~10-100 microseconds to context-switch, hard limit of a few thousand per process.

quiz.question: What is the difference between long polling and SSE?
options: Short polling: the client sends GET /messages every N seconds (say 5s); the server responds immediately with whatever is queued (possibly empty); the client waits 5s and asks again.
Flask's default dev server (app.run()) is single-threaded and synchronous — it processes one request at a time.
For server-to-client push of stock prices to 100k browsers, SSE is the right answer, not long polling and not WebSockets.
Long polling: client GETs /poll?since=N; server holds the response open; when data is ready, server writes the body (typically JSON) and closes the response; client immediately re-GETs.
quiz.explanation: Both deliver server push over plain HTTP, but the mechanics differ. Long polling: client GETs /poll?since=N; server holds the response open; when data is ready, server writes the body (typically JSON) and closes the response; client immediately re-GETs. Each "push" is one full HTTP request-response cycle with all headers repeated.
